utterances.text: Are you referring to any specific situation when the company commander is absent or are you asking me a general question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a general question. When one commander gives up his right to command, does it have to be put in writing? When this right is transferred on to somebody else, does it have to be in writing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: In any case this requires a paper, a document, because the commanding officer of any unit is appointed by a written document, and as from then his duties are prescribed by the law. At the moment when he signs this document on assuming responsibility, that means that this officer assumes the responsibility for everything that happens in his unit, and he also is given legal prerogatives and authorisation to undertake any measure to bring the situation in the unit up to the required level of combat readiness. The moment this right is denied to him as a rule, it should be done in writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lackovic. I am bringing to an end my examination-in-chief today with a conclusion. Do you know Mr. Jokic, and if you do how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, I know Mr. Jokic. I've known him briefly from 1980 when I was completing my military high school and he was finishing his military academy education. We happened to be in the same barracks. This is when I got to know him superficially. After that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I -- Your Honour, I'm objecting as using this witness as it appears they're going into the area of character based on knowledge. And I believe the Court asked Mr. Jokic to make a choice. I may be wrong, but I thought you made a choice. Is he a character witness that knows him or is he an expert giving his opinion? Now we're combining the two. If it's very brief -- but if we're going into it in detail, I just don't think based on the Court's ruling, or based on the relevancy, that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, before we heard this witness we have already made a ruling in this aspect. I hope any questions in this direction will not affect the impartiality of this expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was aiming for the opposite, not for what Mr. McCloskey is saying. But I will finish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lackovic, the fact that you knew Mr. Jokic, did that have any influence on you, on your professional integrity, on your professional career and your professional knowledge, and did that maybe lead you to say something that is not correct and to compromise any of these things?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if the Court allows me, I would like to complete what I was saying. The second time, after 12 years, again --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Not responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I think you have to answer the question put by Mr. Stojanovic here. We are doing a question and answer proceeding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I apologise. Mr. Stojanovic, my acquaintance with Mr. Jokic, I dare say, is not superficial but it is not such that I could come to any decisions about his character. That was not the objective of my analysis or any of my other aspects of work and should not have had any influence on my position on this specific matter. And it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide on his culpability. It is up to me just to state my opinion on some relevant military issues that pertain to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the question was this: Did this acquaintance with Dragan Jokic in any way affect your position and the opinion that you voiced today before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stojanovic. When I was working on the report, I was not affected by any emotional matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more question. I think that in your CV -- we didn't say it, did you attend training and education in Holland in the course of this year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. I attended some training in the Netherlands in Ede in the training school for intelligence personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who organised this training and what kind of a training did you receive. What were you actually preparing for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: The initiative for the training was launched by the Royal Dutch Ministry of Defence. I was in a group of ten officers, senior-ranking officers, of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro who went to the SMID centre in Ede in order to learn English and to prepare for the forthcoming Euro-Atlantic integration processes as well as the joining of Serbia and Montenegro in the partnership for peace programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that this mission, this preparation for peacekeeping operations and Euro-Atlantic integration, was something you completed in a professional manner?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that the whole group, including myself, carried out our duties in a professional way at this training centre for intelligence personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lackovic. I have no more questions for you. Could you please concentrate now in your answers to the questions which will be put to you by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas, Mr. McCloskey from the Prosecution, and possibly from the Judges. And I thank you once again for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Any questions, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have a few general questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to pick up on the last issue, the issue of your education. Could you please tell us after completing the secondary high school, the secondary school for military, how many actual years of military education do you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Following my completion of the military high school, I completed the military academy which took six semesters or three years to complete. I completed the school for the staff -- command staff from 1994 to 1996. This school lasted for two years. As well as the school for national defence. That training took one year. Beside that - and this is not stated in my CV - I also completed some courses at a lower level which were focused on the implementation of some secondary duties in the command staff. Altogether that amounts to about seven years of education and training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And could you please tell us on average how many years of field experience do you have.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, my entire military career was practically based on my work in the field, practical work. Even when I worked as the chief of engineers in the corps, the role of an engineers officer is to follow the unit as it is carrying out its duty out in the field. If I can determine how long this period was, I would say that it was about ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I take it that the rules that you have been commenting on today, those are the same rules that you were trained in and that you applied in the field so you both have theoretical knowledge and practical application knowledge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. The majority of the documents comes from that period, even though a part of those documents was changed. But the substance has remained the same. Through my regular work and training I received practical and theoretical knowledge, including all the -- and I followed all the innovations and amendments in the rules and regulations because these changes were very important in the implementation of my establishment duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that throughout these years you've developed a particular knowledge and expertise in the application -- the interpretation of and the application of these particular rules sufficient enough for you to give an expert opinion to the honourable members of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I believe that I have enough experience, knowledge. This was also confirmed in the process of my schooling, especially the education, the training, that I completed over the past year. So that all the knowledge that I acquired and training in that school give me the grounds for thinking the way I do about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know a little bit about the grading system and the promotional system in this part of the world. And I look at your age, you're -- you seem to be 43, 44, somewhere in that neighbourhood. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You are correct, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair for me to say that based on your grade, which is colonel, and -- you're fairly young to have achieved that grade? Don't be modest.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, I don't think that I'm too old. But in any case for some regular circumstances, you could conclude that I am young. I agree with what you have said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the fact that you were promoted so rapidly could also attest to the fact that perhaps you are extremely competent, because normally promotions don't come too easily in the military. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. The position and the rank that I hold at the moment and the duty that I am performing, I went through all the requisite duties and carried out all the requisite tasks, and my superior officers always graded me well for my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to just focus a couple of questions on your experience as a commander. Could you just please tell us what's the largest amount of people or units that you've commanded so we have an understanding of your positions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. The highest command post that I held was the duty of the commander of the 305th Engineers' Brigade of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro. If we exclude my current position, the deputy commander of the military district of Belgrade, which is not the same rank of the Chief of Staff, which we do not have in our command anyway, but it is of adequate rank. So in commanding the 305th Engineers' Brigade, under my command I had, depending on the period, from several hundred up to 1.000 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just briefly so we have an understanding, what exactly does the 305th Engineers' Brigade do? I don't believe you've commented on that in your direct. But just give us a sense of their mission.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. The 305th Engineers' Brigade is the highest-ranking joint engineers unit of an independent formation in the Army of Serbia and Montenegro. It comprises a command, staff units, just like the majority of other land forces units. It also has engineers battalions. In the brigade that I commanded, there were two pioneers' battalions, one road and bridge construction battalion, a battalion for fortifications, and there was also a camouflage company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just focusing your attention to another area that you -- that was brought up, you talked a little bit about mobilisation. And I wanted to ask you if you are aware of - which you must - of the concept or the doctrine of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Karnavas. That was a doctrine on which the concept of defence of the former SFRY was based. Before that, it was also in force during all the developments from 1990 to 1995. This was a state strategy or a state doctrine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this started at the academy and was this being applied?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. We learned about the doctrine of All People's Defence through the course of our education and training. This was also written about a lot, not only in the press but also in expert publications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned now the year 1995 as a cut-off date. Is that because of the Dayton Accords and the reorganisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible that that is one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just my final question, I guess: Would it be possible for someone, an analyst, an expert, to understand and appreciate what was -- the application of the rules and to interpret the events as they were unfolding throughout this war without fully knowing and appreciating and of course factoring in to their analysis the doctrine of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Vague and calls for speculation. And there's no foundation, and the foundation for that question would take us all the rest of the week and is really not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, just please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You want to rephrase it or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't think it's vague. It's fairly concrete. Secondly, we have testimony from Mr. Butler who admittedly said that to him it wasn't an important concept, and he knew very little of it, and it is on the record. Now I'm asking for this gentleman to comment, is it possible for someone to interpret the events on the ground as they were unfolding. In general. I'm not speaking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: With the understanding that it's a hypothetical question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you may put to this witness. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is just a thinly veiled personal attack on Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not relevant. Enough of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's forget the other experts in the Prosecution's case. Do not mention it at all. Just put a hypothetical question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I understand. However, these antics are unprofessional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well. Put your question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible for an expert to truly understand and interpret the events as they were unfolding during this war - and I'm talking about a foreign expert - if that expert were not to understand, appreciate, and factor into his analysis the doctrine of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He's throwing all this rhetorical -- I don't even know in English what you call it. Understand, appreciate -- these thinly veiled comments about Mr. Butler. Is this necessary at this stage of the game? It's absolutely absurd. It should not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, I think, you know, Mr. Karnavas is obsessed with the term of All People's Defence from the very beginning of this trial. This is maybe the last expert witness in the sense of the military terms. If we did not allow him to put this question to this witness, maybe in the rebuttal or rejoinder cases there will be a big problem. So based on the hypothetic basis, we allowed this question to be put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to go on the record for objecting, Your Honour, and I just want to make this very clear, because I have no objection whatsoever about the All People's Defence. It's the comments that he's interjecting, the unnecessary remarks, about Mr. Butler. I'm just sick and tired of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In my own defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Stop, you, Mr. Karnavas. I agree with Mr. McCloskey that we should not attack anybody in putting any questions. So be very careful to chose the words you are going to use --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, "foreign," what is this kind of talk --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entitled to respond. A foreign expert would not have grown up with this concept and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's not debate on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have to finish this witness as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying, Your Honour. I'm trying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember the question or would you like me to phrase it one more time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember it, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you kindly explain it for us. Give us your answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I believe that an analysis made by any expert insufficiently acquainted with the system of All People's Defence would not be convincing enough and would not present the true state of affairs and facts without dwelling on the matter of whether the expert knew the topic well or not. Without deep analysis and knowledge of the system and how it functioned in all of its segments, it is difficult to be objective and to make a valuable, true analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And one could even jump to conclusions, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. Because conclusions are the products of analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you very, very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Any cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a bit about your experience. Aside from the very unfortunate and I'm sure horrible experience of the NATO bombing, do you have any combat experience?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of combat experience specifically are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any experience in the army during wartime fighting the enemy. I would direct you to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is vague --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The events of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is vague. Does he mean hand-to-hand combat? Does he mean charging up a particular line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the question is quite clear. Any experience during the wartime fighting the enemy. The witness could give his explanations. I think it's specific enough. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted to clarify if this refers to combat in the Army of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina or generally refers to combat. I think Yugoslavia did have certain military experiences and this is known. It's known in which period this was. This was the attack of the NATO forces and the conflict in Kosovo. So the question whether this expert has experience in the Army of Republika Srpska or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think that it seems to me that that would be the proper framework for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all I don't think it's relevant because just the general knowledge from the very beginning of his military service until now. Secondly, I believe that Mr. McCloskey would like to be more specific in terms of the time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're a relatively young guy, man, and there hasn't been -- you know, we haven't fought continuously in this century, so hopefully there's not too many wars. So can you -- I think you understand me. What kind of combat experience have you had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in the NATO air campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1991 [as interpreted] in the entire territory of the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia excluding Kosovo. The whole territory was a combat zone, and I was mostly engaged in the implementation and organisation of tasks to alleviate and clear up the damage caused by NATO bombing. For the engineers, this is a very valuable experience, which I'm sure you will agree is not something that many senior officers have a chance to do in other armies. So for me, this was a valuable experience. As far as my participation is concerned in combat operations such as the ones mentioned by your colleagues, no, I did not take part in combat operations in Republika Srpska, nor did I take part in infantry combat operations anywhere else because that simply wasn't my role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, is there anything you need for clarification in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wish only to draw your attention to line 66 -- that is page 66, line 1. It says that the expert says he had experience in the NATO air campaign in 1991. It's a historical fact that this was not in 1991. The witness mentioned another year. So for the sake of the record, I think this should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, which year did you mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes we're losing track of NATO and their various campaigns. But you're meeting with NATO now. You're coming to Holland and meet with former adversaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you a little bit about the chief of engineers job. And we have heard repeatedly regarding the job of chief of engineers or it could be chief of artillery or chief of security, that it is their job to make proposals to their commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And make plans pursuant to the commander's orders on their proposals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: In essence, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then the commander's orders go out to the -- in this case it would be the engineering company of a brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those would be coming from and initiated by the commander of the brigade or the Chief of Staff which is usually in charge of engineering?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Orders to subordinate units are always issued by the commander. If he is absent, then the Chief of Staff takes on the function of commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think you yourself said that in engineering -- in a brigade the engineer is -- chief of engineers is under the Chief of Staff. You're familiar with that structure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. The chief of engineers in the chain of command is subordinated to the Chief of Staff. He is in the organ dealing with branches and arms of service in the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you testified that in most cases the engineering orders actually come from the Chief of Staff because they are the ones that are working together, but that they can in some situations come from the commander himself. I believe I'm paraphrasing roughly what you said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. I'm afraid you misunderstood this. All orders come from the commander. Proposals for the making of these decisions contained in the order are made by the chief of engineers through the Chief of Staff to the commander. If the commander is absent, then we go a step lower. There is one link less. Then it's the chief of engineers making proposals directly to the Chief of Staff. The Chief of Staff then makes a decision. But he then is acting as the commander. He is the commander in that case because the commander is absent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that all orders will and do -- are responsible for the commander and mist originate there. I thought you were saying, though, that even when the commander is present in the everyday workings of an engineering unit, sometimes the Chief of Staff may issue orders directly to the engineering company without the commander's involvement. The commander of the brigade, that is. So am I not correct on that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I do not exclude the possibility that an order might be issued, but in practice this is not very likely. Because if the commander is there, there is no reason for him not to issue the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the way these bodies such that I've described basically work. The commander is really involved on a brigade level, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's the commander who makes decisions based on proposals by his subordinates. The Chief of Staff is subordinated to him, and the Chief of Staff puts together all the proposals by the various organs of the staff command and ultimately proposes to the commander what the decision should be, or he gives him several options, several versions or variants of the final decision if there is more than one option. Then it's the Chief of Staff who explains these various possibilities and proposes to the commander which option he believes should be selected. He has his favorite option.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to the chief of engineering responsibility as you've described it. We've talked briefly about their responsibility to make proposals and plans, and you said that sometimes those proposals may get corrected by the commander or sometimes even rejected. And then you also -- you said the next step along the way was that the chief of engineers would work out any documents that were indispensable and necessary to the carrying out of the order. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you said that, and I quote you, I believe: "This is where his role is finished, exhausted." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: At the planning stage, yes, that's what I said. That's where his role is exhausted. I'm referring to the planning stage for combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So he's got a lot more to do regarding the carrying out of the commander's orders, doesn't he, the chief of engineers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with that, Mr. McCloskey. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I noted in your report you really didn't talk about that. You didn't get past the planning stage in any great degree. So let's do that. If we could get Exhibit D23/3. And if we could put the English on the ELMO. And if we could focus the ELMO, certainly the last third of the page, that first page, and blow that up a bit. Okay. I won't go over all of this, but we can see there a few lines up from the bottom that it talks about: "Suggests the commander how the directly subordinated engineering units and combat technical resources thereof should be used." And then it says: "Pursuant to the commander's decisions and cooperating and consulting with other organs of the command it proposes tasks of the engineering units, makes a plan, prepares orders." Do you see that in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's what you've been talking about in your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't talk about this segment. I was talking about the planning stage. The work of the chief of engineers at the stage of implementation is something we have touched upon in response to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to spend a whole lot of time on it, but I do want to go -- implementation is a pretty important topic, as you imagine, knowing some of these facts as you do. Let's go down, it's a few lines passed where it says: "Pursuant to the commander's decisions, cooperating and consulting." And it begins: "Controls execution of tasks issued to subordinate engineering units." So it's the job of the chief of engineers to control the execution of the tasks that the commander has issued to the subordinate engineering units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what "control" means in this context.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Control is a planning function carried out by the organs of the staff command in order to assure themselves that the subordinate units are doing exactly what the commander ordered and in the manner that he ordered; that is, that they are complying with the commander's order. Control is implemented on the basis of a plan of control which is drawn up by the organ for operative and teaching tasks of -- operations and training tasks of the brigade. And all the command organs of the brigade, provided that the plan envisages their carrying out control, that is, control is left open as a possibility but it is not a duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This lists a duty. Paragraph 40 it says: "Duties of the engineering organ are as follows." It doesn't say possible duties.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says: "Controls execution of tasks." Now, you said that, yeah, it's his job to make sure the task is carried out pursuant to the commander's orders. So in that job, can the chief of engineers issue an order consistent with the commander's orders to the engineering company commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. McCloskey. The chief of engineers does not have the right to issue orders. He cannot issue any orders regardless of whether such orders relate to the commander's idea or not. By your leave, Mr. McCloskey, I spoke of the role of all the organs of command in the system of control and, within this context, of the place and role of the chief of engineers. It is true that the duty to carry out control and monitoring is prescribed in the rules, but it is also correct that this is not an individual duty left to chance. It is a management function of command. In order to organise control, the command that made the plans is responsible for organising control. Therefore, a command organ cannot go to a subordinate unit if this is not in compliance with the commander's order or if it is not part of the plan approved by the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the chief of engineers cannot direct or tell the engineering company how to do the job according to the commander's orders? He certainly can do that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he can, Mr. McCloskey. All issues that have to do with his profession, yes. But as regards the use made of the unit in combat, that he cannot do. One of the duties and authorities, powers, of the chief of engineers, as I explained, is to look after the combat readiness of the unit. In the professional sense he can do that, but he does not have the right to command the unit or to use it in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't have any disagreement on the right to command. Perhaps when I say "issue orders," you think I'm talking about originating the issue of an order pursuant to a commander. I'm not. When I say issue an order, I mean he is -- well, the first way he can issue an order is to pass on the order of a commander. The commander wants a bridge built at point Y, the chief of engineers tells the commander of the engineering companies, "The commander wants you to build that bridge on point Y, do that." That's passing on the commander's order. The chief of engineers has the right to do what I just said, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. McCloskey. You're right. The chief of engineers does have the right to transmit the commander's order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if the -- and building that bridge the engineers commander picks pine as his material, the chief of engineers can say, "No, I want you to use oak." The chief of engineers can do that, too, can't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are professional matters, strictly professional. And therefore he can express his influence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go down a little farther. It's several lines up from the bottom, and it says: "During combat activities the organ monitors and directs actions of engineering actions in accordance with the commander's decisions." So this says the chief of engineers can direct the actions of the engineering company as long as it's consistent with the decision of the commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: No, sir. In the original it says the following: "During combat operations and activities, the organ directs actions of engineering units in accordance with the commander's decision, suggests to the commander changes and amendments in the tasks issued to the units." We're not speaking of command and control here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: He simply monitors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, are there any translation problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think this is a fundamental issue here. Mr. McCloskey is obviously hearing in the interpretation what suits him, and that is the word "direction." In the B/C/S, in the original, it doesn't say "rukovditi." [phoen] It says "usmjeravati."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And interpreters note that both of these terms can be interpreted as "direction" in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how this will be interpreted, to be quite sincere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They both mean "direct" in English, according to the translation people, and I'm not suggesting we're commanding here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But that does not help. We can look into, to see if there are two different meanings for those two different words in the military context. It's a little late in the day to be bringing this up, and we will look into that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I am again -- I am not suggesting he is a commander and I'm not suggesting he is directing with the extreme responsibility of a commander. But when it says: "Directs the action of," that means that he is influencing the carrying out of the operation, is that correct, no matter which way you translate it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. But we have to put a comma behind this. This is the way in which he implements this. And this is very significant. In order to understand what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The placement of a comma. Have you been listening to President Clinton?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with pleasure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought that sounded familiar. Okay. So if this job is not a bridge-building job and it's an illegal job, it's an improper job, it's part of a process to commit and cover up a crime, when a chief of engineers knowingly directs, as it suggests here, influences the way an illegal job is carried out, he bears some responsibility, in the military sense, for going along with that illegal job, doesn't he, whether he was ordered to do it or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, provided that anyone, not just the chief of engineers, knew that carrying out a certain job constituted a crime and didn't take any measures to prevent it, yes, then he does bear part of the responsibility for it. I repeat, provided that he knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think we'll leave that up to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Any re-direct, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, I only wish to remove the interpretation issue and clear it up very briefly. Re-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lackovic, in the B/C/S when describing the duties of the chief of engineers, there was a word used "usmjerava."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Stojanovic. That's what I read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the notion of "usmjeravati" imply necessarily that the person exercising command and control issues orders on the work of the command staffs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go step by step. Does "usmjeravati" a unit -- is this something that only the person exercising command and control can do, or can it also be done by someone with no command and control responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your question is clear to me now. In the process of decision-making there is a decision, and there are corrective decisions. Both notions fall under the competence of the commander. The commander reached a decision, he has the right to reach a corrective decision, and he issues this decision pursuant to reports from the field which he receives from his organs or from his immediately subordinate commanders. That's what I was trying to point out. So the manner in which "usmjeravanje" is carried out is important. By gaining insight into the situation on the ground, the chief of a branch or arm of service proposes to the commander through the regular channels that a corrective decision should be made by the commander. How reliable the information that the chief of a branch gets from the ground is a different issue. If he is sent to monitor the situation on the ground himself, then of course this information is reliable. If he receives this information through the duty system or through the chain of command, then the information is less reliable and less self-evident. In any case, the manner of "usmjeravanje," of the activities of a conditionally speaking subordinate unit, because the unit is not subordinated to the chief of the branch but to the commander, is again carried out through the regular channels. Based on an insight into the manner of carrying out combat assignments on the ground, the chief of a branch proposes to the commander either that implementation should be continued or that the decision should be corrected and an amended order be issued. In practice, we have corrective decisions made by the commander and expressed through combat orders. Therefore, the commander's order can be corrected during the implementation of combat activities by means of a combat order. This constitutes a correction of the original decision, and this is what we mean when we say "usmjeravanje" of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just conclude by asking you whether you still abide by your fundamental thesis that the chief of engineers does not command and control the use of an engineering unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. In the sense that you mean, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to repeat my question because of the interpretation again. Can the chief of engineers at any time in accordance with the regulations have the command of -- have the duty of direction and the responsibility of command towards an engineering unit, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the commander authorises him in writing for this and when his -- this duty is regulated in writing, otherwise no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lackovic. And to conclude, you told Mr. McCloskey that the chief of engineers can pass on orders to the commander or komandir of an engineering company. In accordance with paragraph 114 of the regulations already mentioned by you in emergency situations in states of war and so on, the commander can issue an order directly to the komandir of an engineering company, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's his right to issue direct orders to his subordinates, not just the commander of a company but anyone in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And to conclude, does the duty operations officer at the time he is carrying out this duty, can he also be the chief of the functional service that he belongs to? Can he perform both duties at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he cannot, Mr. Stojanovic. And that is regulated in the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask one more question on an area that was brought up, this important area regarding the direction and the meaning -- the two meanings of it. Just one question. I've been very brief, as you know, in all my crosses. If you could just give me this. There is one question related to one short document that's already in evidence that I think will help with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But please bear in mind that your question will be subject to re-direct if there's any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It should be the same subject relatively. It may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- cause a little more discussion, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit 513/B. We can put the English on the ELMO. Further cross-examination by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know you're familiar with these documents from your review. This is a page, 14 July, out the daily order book of the engineering company. This is the day, as I know you're aware, that Major Jokic was the duty officer. And looking at number 5 entitled: "Tasks received from brigade command." It says: "Ostoja Djuric is to be appointed officer for technical services and supplies by the order of the chief of engineer." Is this order from Mr. Jokic? Which kind of direction is this, the one with the U or the other one or neither?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to this particular wording that by order of the chief of engineers Ostoja Djuric is to be appointed officer for technical service and supplies? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I said. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this does not have any legal effect. As far as I can see, this was assigned by company commander. But nowhere in the documents did I come across an order by -- this would have been regulated because any appointment is regulated by the order on appointment signed by the brigade commander for non-commissioned officers and corps commander or higher-ranking officer for officers, or even the chief of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska army for officers. So I wouldn't be able to say what this was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, do you want to re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think I've had enough excitement for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, colonel. I have one question as a matter of clarification I think. When you were talking this morning about resubordination you made an example and you told us that a military unit could be resubordinated to a civilian Territorial Defence unit. I've heard always the things the other way around, the civilians were subordinated to the military. But this is the first time I hear about a military unit resubordinated to a civilian organ. Can you clarify that for me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was talking about resubordination of military units and I explained this on an example. It is correct that it is customary for all the structures in the area of defence to be put in the function of carrying out defence activities to the extent to which it has been provided for by the decisions of state bodies. In this particular case when it comes to sending and resubordination of an individual or a technical equipment to a body that belongs to the civilian structure, be it a unit that is -- that consists of people on work obligation or the civilian protection unit. In my view and in practice, that should not be anything out of the ordinary. I don't think that this is contrary to any rules or regulations or that it is out of the ordinary for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Argibay. Any questions out of Judge's questions? Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Further cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In determining whether or not a unit was in fact subordinated -- a military unit was subordinated to a civilian structure, would you want to know what task the unit was carrying out in order to determine whether it was a military task or a civilian task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean whether I personally would be interested in that in my capacity as a commander of such a unit maybe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your capacity as an expert witness trying to sort out whether or not this was a civilian-managed operation and the military was merely subordinated to this civilian operation, or whether this was a military-run operation where the civilians were working for the military, as the Judge had opined it to you, the possibilities of the two things. Would you want to know what that task was to help you determine that? I mean, for example, if the task ended up being the engineers helping bury the local refuse that had built up over the winter, that sounds like a civilian task as opposed to whether or not the operation had to do specifically with prisoners of war. Wouldn't that be a factor in figuring out who was actually in charge or running this task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSAV LACKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Probably it would be important if we were talking about a unit. In that case, it would be important and it would merit attention. Bearing in mind that only one person and one piece of equipment were engaged on simple tasks, to my mind, the tasks such as excavations, I don't think it is important and that it doesn't deserve any attention. The command was not to be too concerned with such a simple engagement. Because it was not resubordination of an entire unit but rather of an individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you're not familiar with the job that is the basis of that hypothetical. So I don't think I need any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage are there any documents to tender? Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We would like to tender the rules of service in the armed forces as D71/3 and the regulations on the authorities of the command as D72/3. And I would also like to thank the interpreters, because in preparing for today's hearing they had to translate both of these documents into English. As for D74/3, I would like to tender the CV of Mr. Lackovic. And in my conversation with Mr. McCloskey I got his agreement to do that, that we should make indisputable some of the paragraphs that can be found in the expert's written report if at all possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can't tell from what Mr. Stojanovic said what D71/3 and D72/3 are. We have some rules, and I think they're the rules we're talking about, but until we can confirm that we're not really sure exactly what he means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. The issue is that, Mr. Stojanovic, did you furnish those translations to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is the rules that we have been talking about, and now I hear that the translation has still not been provided to Mr. McCloskey. And two weeks ago we sent the rules for translation to the translation service. If there's anything disputable, I accept that. Mr. McCloskey should voice his opinion on that after having received this translation. And later in the course of the day we're going to check what has happened with the translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Given that we are familiar with engineering rules and rules of the duty officer that are already in evidence, that's what we're a little confused on. Because that's already in evidence. So this is new material we haven't seen. As Mr. Stojanovic says, it's merely reprints of the JNA rules. If that's what it is, I'm sure I will have no objection, but I generally like to see what it is before I agree to it going into evidence. So with that proviso, we don't have any problem. With the report, I know the Court is aware of my concerns as I indicated them first thing, and now of course I am aware of the Court's concerns on that same subject. And given that the witness has testified, I do have serious problems with this report coming in at all. Though I did promise Mr. Stojanovic, and I will work with him to look at that report to see if we can identify statements of rules and expert opinions that are not arguments and are not legal arguments, and if we can find that, I will -- we'll get back to you and reach a stipulated agreement about that for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no objection to the CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification on the report itself. We're constantly told, you know, Your Honour, that because we're before Professional Judges, the Judges can very well throw out what they don't want, what they don't find acceptable. So I think the Court can very well redact on its own what it thinks is not relevant or its -- it invades the province of the Judges. So that's why we allow a lot of evidence to come in, and it's up to the Trial Chamber to decide what, if any, weight to give it. So I don't really see the point of that. But if there is going to be redaction, I would suggest that it be done the other way around, that is, take out the opinions and the body remain the way it is. I have read the report, and frankly I don't have a problem with it myself. But I understand the concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the standing of Mr. Karnavas. Unless Mr. Jokic or counsel specifically designates him the authority to argue regarding his exhibits, that is not appropriate and may not be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, as for the document D74/3, the CV of this witness is admitted into the evidence. The document D71/3, D72/3 we temporarily made a decision to admit it into evidence at this stage, pending the translations of those documents and we still give the opportunity for the Prosecution to check these regulations, whether we have already admitted it or not, whether it's part of the whole regulation or not, you know, for these kind of things. As for the document D73/1, the suggestions by Mr. Karnavas might be the last result. But since the two parties agree to put their heads together to work out some redactions on those reports, I believe that we give this in a priority to the parties to decide. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I was merely speaking as an amici, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that. I understand that. I'm not going to dwell on this issue any longer since time is up. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, concerning with the future witnesses, are there any matters that Mr. Stojanovic or Mr. Lukic would like to inform us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we have already informed you, tomorrow we have two witnesses. The first one should take just one session and the second witness which will be a character witness should take even less than that. So I hope and I have informed the Prosecution team that we will be able to finish both witnesses tomorrow. We have not planned any protective measures for any of the two witnesses tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll resume tomorrow morning 9.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
